newsitem.title: UK: Coffee prices in fresh rally as supply woes linger.
newsitem.headline: Coffee prices in fresh rally as supply woes linger.

text.p: World coffee markets, stirred by concerns about Latin American supply and low consumer stocks, soared upto 16 percent this week led by U.S. futures of arabica type beans.
Analysts said the gains could be sustained ahead of the Brazilian frost season which begins in June.
"What goes up has to come down but in this case, nobody is willing to sell because the market could rally again," said one London trader.

On Thursday, New York coffee futures prices, boosted by shortages of arabica beans -- the premium coffee -- from Latin America, rocketed to new highs since the last devastating Brazilian frosts in June and July 1994.
Traders said Thursday's frenzied buying was triggered by concerns about shrinking U.S. warehouse stocks.
Coffee was trading about $1 per pound in early December when worries about dwindling stocks at roasters (processors) began to cause buying of futures by speculators and merchants.
By Thursday, the benchmark July coffee futures traded to a high of $2.24 per pound before closing the day at $2.22, up 12.50 cents.

The sky-rocketing prices triggered a fresh retail price rise by leading U.S. coffee roaster Folgers this week. On Friday, large German roaster Kraft Jacobs Suchard said it would not rule out further retail price increases.
London's futures for robusta type beans, used mainly in the manufacture of soluble or instant coffee, have also risen sharply since early January before peaking in early March.
By Friday, the July contract was hovering at $1,660 a tonne, still up from around $1,200 in early January but down from its March peak of 1,820.
Unlike arabicas, robusta beans are in good supplies.

New York futures rose above $2 on March 5, the first time they had topped this level since the last big crop-damaging frost in top grower Brazil in 1994, after rising from a cyclical low around $1.15 on January 2.
Commodity brokerage GNI Ltd said in a commentary on Friday that the market still has the Brazil frost season to contend with.
"...(It) should limit how far prices can fall in the medium term," it said.
Fresh supplies from Colombia and Central American states are tight due to seasonal factors and heavy sales already made by producers to take advantage of the blistering rally in prices.
"Relief from the high prices is not likely to come before July," Merrill Lynch said in a bi-weekly report released this week.

"Seasonally, the market generally retreats from mid-July onwards if there is no frost in Brazil, but given the lack of availability the market might stay firm, especially if the 1997/98 Colombian crop is going to be delayed as sources in that country predict," the U.S. brokerage said.
Analysts said further retail price hikes could slow consumption and prevent a re-stocking by roasters.
"Consumers may go for cheaper coffee blends or give up drinking (coffee) altogether. Anyway coffee is not a staple item," said one.
